question: Alec controls [Elspeth Conquers Death] and puts the third lore counter it. With the triggered ability, they target [Eternal Witness] in their graveyard. When Eternal Witness returns to the battlefield, can it target Elspeth Conquers Death with its trigger?
answer:
Yes. By the time Eternal Witness's enters-the-battlefield trigger is put on the stack and its target is chosen, Elspeth Conquers Death is already a card in Alec's graveyard, so it's a legal target and can be returned to Alec's hand.

Why the timing works out:

- The third lore counter triggers Elspeth Conquers Death's chapter III ability, a triggered ability that goes on the stack and targets a creature or planeswalker card in the graveyard — here, Eternal Witness [Elspeth Conquers Death ruling #2].
- Chapter III resolves and Eternal Witness enters the battlefield, which triggers Eternal Witness's "When this creature enters, you may return target card from your graveyard to your hand."
- Once the chapter III ability has left the stack (by resolving), Alec sacrifices Elspeth Conquers Death as a state-based action, because its lore counters equal its greatest chapter number. This doesn't use the stack [Elspeth Conquers Death ruling #11]. Elspeth Conquers Death goes to Alec's graveyard.
- Eternal Witness's trigger isn't put on the stack until the next time a player would receive priority, and its target is chosen at that moment, as the ability is put on the stack [115.1d]. At that point Elspeth Conquers Death is a card in the graveyard, so Alec may choose it as the target. This mirrors the principle in [Eternal Witness ruling #0], where Eternal Witness's ability can target a card that hit the graveyard as part of the same resolution that put Eternal Witness onto the battlefield.

Two practical notes: the ability says "you may," so Alec still chooses on resolution whether to actually return the Elspeth Conquers Death card to hand — but the target must be locked in when the trigger goes on the stack [115.1d]. And if for some reason Elspeth Conquers Death were not sacrificed (for instance, lore counters had been removed so it hadn't reached its final chapter [Elspeth Conquers Death ruling #5]), it would still be a permanent on the battlefield and thus not a legal target for Eternal Witness, which only targets cards in a graveyard.

This works the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Yes.

After this, triggers are placed onto the stack, and Elspeth Conquers Death is in the graveyard able to be the target of Eternal Witness's triggered ability.

question: Autumn attacks with [Robber of the Rich], exiling [Light Up the Stage] from Nehemiah's library. Can Autumn pay Light Up the Stage's Spectacle cost with only {C}?
answer:
Yes — Autumn can pay Light Up the Stage's spectacle cost of {R} using one {C}, provided an opponent has lost life this turn and it's a legal time to cast a sorcery.

Why it works:

- Robber of the Rich's own text says "During any turn you attacked with a Rogue, you may cast that card and you may spend mana as though it were mana of any color to cast that spell." That permission applies to casting Light Up the Stage, whichever cost Autumn pays for it. Robber of the Rich is a Rogue and Autumn attacked with it, so the permission is active this turn (and it keeps applying on later turns Autumn attacks with a Rogue — Robber of the Rich ruling #5).
- "Spend mana as though it were mana of any color" only changes how Autumn may pay the cost; it doesn't change the cost itself or what mana was actually spent [609.4b]. So the {C} (colorless mana specifically, which normally can never pay a colored symbol) is spent as though it were {R} and satisfies the spectacle symbol. The cost is still {R}, not {C}.
- Spectacle is a static ability functioning on the stack that means "You may pay [cost] rather than pay this spell's mana cost if an opponent lost life this turn," and it follows the alternative-cost rules [702.137a]. Light Up the Stage's spectacle cost is {R} — one red mana and nothing else, no generic component — so a single {C} spent as red pays it in full.

Two conditions Autumn still has to meet:

1. An opponent must have lost life at some point this turn [702.137a]. Simply attacking with Robber of the Rich doesn't do that; combat damage to Nehemiah in the combat damage step would (damage dealt to a player causes that much life loss — Light Up the Stage ruling #4). Spectacle only cares that life was lost this turn, not that the life total is still lower (Light Up the Stage ruling #6), and the cost is {R} no matter how much life was lost or how many opponents lost it (Light Up the Stage ruling #7).
2. Light Up the Stage is a sorcery, and neither spectacle nor Robber of the Rich changes when it can be cast (Light Up the Stage ruling #8, Robber of the Rich ruling #6). Autumn must cast it during their own main phase with an empty stack — realistically the postcombat main phase of this same turn, after damage has been dealt.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Autumn casts Light Up the Stage in the postcombat main phase after Robber of the Rich (or something else) has caused an opponent to lose life. If Autumn instead tries to cast it in the precombat main phase before any opponent has lost life this turn, spectacle isn't available at all and Autumn would have to pay the full mana cost of {2}{R} — where the {C} could pay part of the generic {2}, and, thanks to Robber of the Rich, also the {R}.

Multiplayer note: with more than two players, any opponent losing life turns spectacle on, and the defending player for Robber of the Rich's trigger is whoever is being attacked (or controls the attacked planeswalker — Robber of the Rich ruling #9). Even if the opponent who lost life later leaves the game, spectacle is still available that turn (Light Up the Stage ruling #3).

question: Nico controls [Urza's Saga] with two lore counters on it. Alexzander uses [Jinx] to change its land type. What happens?
answer:
Alexzander's Jinx makes Nico's Urza's Saga a basic land type of Alexzander's choice (say Island) until end of turn. Urza's Saga loses its "Urza's" land type and all abilities from its own rules text — including all three chapter abilities and the intrinsic Saga lore-counter ability — and gains that basic type's mana ability ("{T}: Add {U}" for Island). It keeps the abilities chapters I and II already granted it, and under the current wording of the Saga sacrifice rule it is NOT sacrificed: it just sits there as an enchantment land until end of turn.

Details:

1. Type change (layer 4). Jinx sets Urza's Saga's land subtype. Per rule 305.7, Urza's Saga no longer has its old land type, loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and copiable effects, and gains the mana ability of the new basic land type. It does not gain the "basic" supertype, and it stays an Enchantment Land and stays a Saga (Saga is an enchantment subtype, not a land subtype, so Jinx doesn't touch it) — rules 305.7 and 205.4b.

2. What Urza's Saga keeps. Rule 305.7 expressly does not remove abilities granted by other effects. Chapters I and II already resolved (that's why there are two lore counters), and per Urza's Saga ruling #5 those granted abilities last as long as Urza's Saga is on the battlefield. So Nico's permanent still has "{T}: Add {C}" and "{2}, {T}: Create a 0/0 colorless Construct artifact creature token with 'This token gets +1/+1 for each artifact you control,'" plus the new "{T}: Add {U}" from the Island type. Note {C} and {U} are different mana: {C} is colorless mana specifically and can't be paid with {U}, and neither is "generic."

3. No sacrifice. Rules 704.5s and 714.4 only sacrifice a Saga whose lore counters are at or above its final chapter number if it is "a Saga permanent with one or more chapter abilities." With its rules text gone, Nico's permanent has zero chapter abilities, so that state-based action doesn't apply. (Urza's Saga ruling #1 says a Saga that loses all chapter abilities is immediately sacrificed; that ruling predates the current wording of 704.5s/714.4 quoted above, which added the "with one or more chapter abilities" condition. I'm following the rules text as provided.)

4. No new lore counter while jinxed. The precombat-main-phase turn-based action (rules 505.4 and 703.4f) only puts a lore counter on Sagas with one or more chapter abilities, so nothing would be added while Jinx is in effect. Chapter abilities are the "{rN}—[Effect]" triggers described in rules 107.15a and 714.2b, and the "enters with a lore counter" ability is the intrinsic ability of rule 714.3a — all part of the rules text that's gone for the turn.

5. After the turn ends. Jinx's effect ends during the cleanup step. Urza's Saga gets its Urza's land type, rules text, and chapter abilities back, still with two lore counters. Two is less than its final chapter number (III), so rules 704.5s and 714.4 still don't sacrifice it; on Nico's next precombat main phase it gets its third lore counter, chapter III triggers, and after that trigger leaves the stack Nico sacrifices it (Urza's Saga ruling #4).

Timing assumption: I'm assuming both chapter I and chapter II have already resolved and nothing of Urza's Saga's is on the stack when Jinx resolves. If instead the chapter II trigger were still on the stack when Jinx resolved, that trigger exists independently of its source and would still resolve and grant the Construct-token ability; Urza's Saga would also be "the source of a chapter ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack" for purposes of rules 704.5s and 714.4, which is another reason it wouldn't be sacrificed at that moment.

Player count: nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table. The sacrifice (when it eventually happens) is always by the Saga's controller, Nico, and the lore counter is added only in the controller's own precombat main phase (rules 505.4, 703.4f, 704.5s); Alexzander choosing the basic land type is just the caster of Jinx making its choice.

question: Ada controls [Ethersworn Canonist]. They want to suspend [Shade of Trokair] and then cast [Divination]. Can they?
answer:
Yes — provided Ada hasn't already cast a nonartifact spell earlier this turn, they can suspend Shade of Trokair for {W} and then cast Divination for {2}{U}. The order matters: suspend first, cast Divination second.

Why it works:

1. Exiling a card with suspend is a special action, not casting a spell [116.2f], [Shade of Trokair ruling #7]. So taking the suspend action doesn't itself count as "casting a nonartifact spell" for Ethersworn Canonist, and it doesn't use the stack.
2. However, suspend's static ability only lets Ada exile Shade of Trokair "if you could begin to cast this card by putting it onto the stack from your hand" [702.62a], and rule 702.62c says you must take into account any effects that would prohibit that card from being cast [702.62c]; rule 601.3 says a player can begin to cast a spell only if no rule or effect prohibits it. Ethersworn Canonist's text — "Each player who has cast a nonartifact spell this turn can't cast additional nonartifact spells" — is exactly such a prohibition, and Shade of Trokair is a nonartifact (creature) card. Since Ada has cast no nonartifact spell yet this turn, nothing prohibits them from beginning to cast Shade of Trokair, so the suspend action is legal. Note that the check is only whether Ada *could begin* to cast it, not whether they could actually finish paying for it [Shade of Trokair ruling #2].
3. Timing: Shade of Trokair is a creature card and Divination is a sorcery, so both actions need Ada to have priority during their own main phase with the stack empty [117.1a]. Suspend it first, let the stack be empty, then cast Divination.
4. Divination is then Ada's one allowed nonartifact spell for the turn [Ethersworn Canonist ruling #1].

If the order is reversed: cast Divination first, and Ethersworn Canonist now prohibits Ada from casting additional nonartifact spells this turn. Because Ada could no longer begin to cast Shade of Trokair from hand, they could not take the suspend special action at all that turn [702.62c], [116.2f], [601.3].

One thing to plan for later: when the last time counter is removed from Shade of Trokair, its triggered ability lets Ada *cast* it [702.62a]. That is a real cast of a nonartifact spell, so on that turn Ethersworn Canonist will stop it if Ada has already cast a nonartifact spell that turn (and will stop any other nonartifact spell afterward). Casting Shade of Trokair from exile that way follows the alternative-cost rules [702.62d].

Assumption stated plainly: I'm assuming no nonartifact spell has been cast by Ada earlier this turn. If one has, neither the suspend action nor Divination is possible this turn.

Multiplayer: Ethersworn Canonist restricts "each player" individually, so the answer is identical whether the game has two players or more — Ada's own casts are all that matter for Ada's restriction.

question: Asa controls an [Inventors' Fair], a [Krark-Clan Ironworks], and two [Piston Sledge]. They want to activate the last ability of Inventors' Fair and sacrifice a Piston Sledge to help pay the cost. Is this legal?
answer:
Yes, it's legal. Asa controls exactly three artifacts (Krark-Clan Ironworks and the two Piston Sledge — Inventors' Fair is a land, not an artifact), so the "Activate only if you control three or more artifacts" restriction on Inventors' Fair's last ability is satisfied at the moment of activation. Sacrificing a Piston Sledge afterward to Krark-Clan Ironworks for mana does not retroactively make the activation illegal.

How the sequence works:

1. Asa announces the activation of Inventors' Fair's ability. The artifact-count restriction is checked here, and only here — per [Inventors' Fair ruling #2], the number of artifacts is checked only as you activate the ability and is not checked again on resolution. Three artifacts (Krark-Clan Ironworks, Piston Sledge, Piston Sledge) is enough.
2. The total cost is locked in as {4}, {T}, Sacrifice Inventors' Fair ([601.2h]).
3. During the payment step, Asa may activate mana abilities, since a player may activate an activated mana ability while activating an ability that requires a mana payment, even in the middle of that activation ([605.3a]). Asa activates Krark-Clan Ironworks's ability, sacrificing a Piston Sledge, and adds {C}{C}. Colorless mana can pay generic costs, so that {C}{C} covers two of the {4}.
4. Asa then pays the rest of the {4} (for example, by sacrificing the second Piston Sledge to Krark-Clan Ironworks for another {C}{C}, which finishes the {4} exactly), taps Inventors' Fair as the {T} portion, and sacrifices Inventors' Fair. Note that because {T} is part of the cost, Inventors' Fair cannot also be tapped for {C} with its mana ability. Partial payment isn't allowed, so Asa must be able to cover the full {4} ([601.2h], [118.3]).

One thing to be careful about: each payment applies to only one cost ([118.10]). Sacrificing a Piston Sledge pays Krark-Clan Ironworks's activation cost; the {C}{C} it produces pays part of Inventors' Fair's {4}. Those are two different costs, so this is fine — but the same Piston Sledge can't be sacrificed for two separate costs.

Also, activating mana abilities is never mandatory ([118.3c]), so Asa is free to pay the {4} from lands or other sources instead and keep both Piston Sledge on the battlefield.

This works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

question: Amare controls [Psychogenic Probe] and casts [Pain], targeting Nico. They discard a [Progenitus]. Does Psychogenic Probe trigger?
answer:
Yes — Psychogenic Probe triggers, and it deals 2 damage to Nico.

How it plays out:

1. Amare casts Pain (the {B} half of the split card Pain // Suffering), targeting Nico. Pain resolves and Nico discards a card — the discarded card is Progenitus.
2. Progenitus's own text reads "If Progenitus would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, reveal Progenitus and shuffle it into its owner's library instead." That is a replacement effect: the event of Progenitus going to the graveyard is replaced, and instead Nico (as Progenitus's owner, assuming Nico owns the discarded card) reveals it and shuffles their library. Note that Progenitus's printed text is what governs here, overriding the normal result that a discarded card goes to the graveyard.
3. A shuffle therefore actually happens, and it happens because of a spell/ability (Pain's resolution operating together with Progenitus's static replacement ability). Psychogenic Probe's trigger — "Whenever a spell or ability causes a player to shuffle their library, this artifact deals 2 damage to that player" — is met, so it triggers and deals 2 damage to Nico, the player who shuffled.

A couple of related points:

- Rule 603.2g says an event that's prevented or replaced won't trigger anything. That applies to the "Progenitus is put into a graveyard" event, which never occurs — so nothing that triggers on a card being put into a graveyard triggers here. It does not stop Psychogenic Probe, because the shuffle event genuinely occurs.
- Progenitus's protection from everything doesn't matter: Pain targets the player Nico, not Progenitus, and Psychogenic Probe's damage is dealt to a player, not to Progenitus (see Progenitus ruling #0).
- Even if Nico's library were empty when the shuffle happened, Psychogenic Probe would still trigger (Psychogenic Probe ruling #0).
- Incidentally, Amare casting Pain targeting the opponent Nico is a "crime" under rule 700.13, in case any of Amare's other permanents care.

Player count doesn't change this: Psychogenic Probe deals its 2 damage to whichever player shuffled — here Nico — whether the game is two-player or multiplayer. The provided rules include nothing multiplayer-specific that would alter this.

One assumption worth flagging: if Progenitus were owned by someone other than the discarding player Nico (possible only if the card had changed hands), it would be shuffled into that owner's library instead, and Psychogenic Probe's 2 damage would go to that owner rather than to Nico.

question: Albert controls [Doubling Season] and [Pir, Imaginative Rascal] and activates the +1 ability of [Ajani, Mentor of Heroes]. How many loyalty counters does it gain?
answer:
Ajani, Mentor of Heroes gains 2 loyalty counters: the 1 from the cost itself, plus 1 more from Pir, Imaginative Rascal. Doubling Season does not apply at all.

Why:

1. Doubling Season is out. Doubling Season reads "If an *effect* would put one or more counters on a permanent you control..." Activating a loyalty ability with a [+1] symbol means putting a loyalty counter on Ajani, Mentor of Heroes as a *cost*, not as an effect, so Doubling Season never sees the event. [Doubling Season ruling #4] says exactly this: planeswalkers entering get double loyalty counters, "However, if you activate an ability whose cost has you put loyalty counters on a planeswalker, the number you put on isn't doubled. This is because those counters are put on as a cost, not as an effect."

2. Pir, Imaginative Rascal is in. Pir, Imaginative Rascal reads "If one or more counters *would be put* on a permanent your team controls, that many plus one of each of those kinds of counters are put on that permanent instead." It contains no "an effect would" restriction, so unlike Doubling Season it applies to the loyalty counter being paid as a cost. Loyalty is a real counter-based characteristic of planeswalkers [306.5b], so "that many plus one" turns the 1 loyalty counter into 2. This card-specific wording is what drives the different result for the two permanents.

3. So the total cost paid is putting 2 loyalty counters on Ajani, Mentor of Heroes, and it will be at 6 loyalty if it started at its printed 4. This is the same for either of Ajani, Mentor of Heroes's two [+1] abilities.

Assumption on order/timing: it doesn't matter here, because only one of the two replacement effects can apply. If both had been applicable, Albert (as controller of the affected permanent) would pick the order to apply them [616.1g], and each effect would only get one shot at the event [614.5] — so "double, then +1" gives 3 and "+1, then double" gives 4. Also note that if Albert controlled other cost-increasing effects on loyalty abilities, all the counter costs would be combined into a single cost first [606.5]; that isn't the case here.

Player count: this works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table. The only multiplayer wrinkle is Pir, Imaginative Rascal's phrase "your team," which matters in team formats like Two-Headed Giant — a teammate's planeswalker would also get the extra loyalty counter.

question: Aminah casts a [Show and Tell]. As it resolves, Aminah chooses to put a [Haru-Onna] onto the battlefield and Nico chooses to put a [Domestication] onto the battlefield enchanting Haru-Onna. Who controls the enters-the-battlefield ability of Haru-Onna?
answer:
Nico controls Haru-Onna's enters-the-battlefield trigger, so Nico draws the card.

Why:

1. Show and Tell puts all the chosen cards onto the battlefield simultaneously — after every player has chosen, the cards enter at the same time [Show and Tell ruling #2], with any choices (such as what Domestication enchants) made in turn order beforehand, active player first [Show and Tell ruling #0]. So there is no moment at which Haru-Onna is on the battlefield without Domestication already attached to it.

2. By default Haru-Onna would enter under Aminah's control, since an effect that instructs a player to put an object onto the battlefield puts it there under that player's control [110.2a]. But Domestication is an Aura that enters attached to Haru-Onna [303.4e] and reads "You control enchanted creature," a control-changing continuous effect. Control-changing effects are applied in layer 2 and apply continuously from the moment the Aura is on the battlefield [613.1b]. Because Domestication and Haru-Onna arrived simultaneously, that effect is already applying the instant Haru-Onna is on the battlefield, so Nico is Haru-Onna's controller from the start.

3. A triggered ability is controlled by the player who controlled its source at the time it triggered [603.3a], [113.8], and this is true even while the ability is waiting to go on the stack [109.4b]. The source is Haru-Onna, which Nico controls, so Nico puts "draw a card" on the stack and Nico draws.

Timing caveat: this assumes the normal Show and Tell sequence, where both permanents enter simultaneously. If instead Domestication somehow arrived after Haru-Onna had already entered (a separate Domestication cast later, for example), Haru-Onna's trigger would have already triggered under Aminah's control and Aminah would draw the card; the control change would only affect things going forward.

Side notes: Aminah remains Haru-Onna's owner [110.2a], so Haru-Onna's second ability, which returns it "to its owner's hand," would send it to Aminah's hand. Domestication's end-step trigger has an intervening "if" clause and won't even trigger while Haru-Onna's power is 2 [Domestication ruling #0].

Multiplayer: nothing here changes with more than two players. Show and Tell lets each player put in a card, with choices made by the active player first and then the others in turn order [Show and Tell ruling #2], and whichever player controls the Domestication enchanting Haru-Onna controls Haru-Onna and therefore its enters-the-battlefield trigger.

question:
Amani controls a [Founding the Third Path], and its third ability is resolving. Amani chooses to cast a [Fatal Push] from their graveyard. Amani currently does not have Revolt.
Can Amani choose to target [Skyhunter Patrol] with Fatal Push? Will Skyhunter Patrol be destroyed by Fatal Push?
answer:
Yes, Amani can target Skyhunter Patrol with Fatal Push — but as things stand Skyhunter Patrol will not be destroyed.

Why targeting is legal: Fatal Push says "Destroy target creature if it has mana value 2 or less." The word "target" is just "target creature," with no mana value restriction on the target itself; the mana value condition is part of the effect, not the targeting requirement. [Fatal Push ruling #3] states plainly that Fatal Push can target any creature, even one with mana value 5 or greater, and that the creature's mana value is checked only as Fatal Push resolves. Skyhunter Patrol is a creature on the battlefield, so it's a legal target (115.2).

Why nothing happens: Skyhunter Patrol has mana cost {2}{W}{W}, so its mana value is 4. When Fatal Push resolves, Skyhunter Patrol is still a legal target, so Fatal Push does resolve (608.2b) — it simply fails its condition. Without Revolt, Fatal Push only destroys the creature if it has mana value 2 or less; 4 is not 2 or less. With Revolt (a permanent left the battlefield under Amani's control this turn) the threshold would be 4 or less, which Skyhunter Patrol would meet.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Amani still has no Revolt at the moment Fatal Push resolves. Revolt is checked on resolution, so if any permanent leaves the battlefield under Amani's control after Fatal Push is cast but before it resolves — a sacrificed artifact, a token dying, a bounced permanent all count [Fatal Push ruling #0][Fatal Push ruling #2] — then Revolt turns on and Skyhunter Patrol (mana value 4) is destroyed. Note that Founding the Third Path's chapter III exiling the Fatal Push card moves it from the graveyard to exile, not from the battlefield, so that does not enable Revolt.

Casting details: Founding the Third Path's chapter III exiles target instant or sorcery card from Amani's graveyard, copies it, and Amani may cast the copy. Amani must cast it right then, during the ability's resolution, and must pay all costs — here {B} for Fatal Push [Founding the Third Path ruling #2].

Crime note: if Skyhunter Patrol is controlled by an opponent, casting Fatal Push targeting it is committing a crime (700.13, Crime). That's true whether the game is two-player or multiplayer; in multiplayer it's a crime as long as the Skyhunter Patrol's controller is one of Amani's opponents, and targeting Amani's own Skyhunter Patrol would not be a crime. Chapter III targeting a card in Amani's own graveyard is likewise not a crime.

question: Ari controls [Bludgeon Brawl] and [Soldevi Digger]. They cast [Titania's Song]. Once it resolves, what are the characteristics of Soldevi Digger?
answer:
Soldevi Digger becomes a 2/2 colorless artifact creature with no abilities and no subtypes — it is NOT an Equipment.

Characteristic by characteristic (the list of characteristics is given in rule [109.3]):
- Name: Soldevi Digger
- Mana cost: {2} (two generic mana; unchanged — no colored or {C} symbols involved)
- Mana value: 2
- Color: colorless (nothing here changes color; {2} is generic, so it produces no color)
- Card types: Artifact Creature (Titania's Song adds the creature type line)
- Subtypes: none — in particular not Equipment, and Titania's Song grants no creature type
- Supertypes: none
- Rules text/abilities: none. Titania's Song removes "{2}: Put the top card of your graveyard on the bottom of your library," and Soldevi Digger never keeps the equip {2} / "Equipped creature gets +2/+0" from Bludgeon Brawl.
- Power/toughness: 2/2 (equal to its mana value of 2)

Why Bludgeon Brawl drops off: Bludgeon Brawl only applies to "each noncreature, non-Equipment artifact." Once Titania's Song makes Soldevi Digger an artifact creature, Bludgeon Brawl's effect simply doesn't apply to it. This is stated directly by [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #2]: if an artifact affected by Bludgeon Brawl later becomes a creature, Bludgeon Brawl's effect no longer applies, that artifact stops being an Equipment, and it becomes unattached from any creature it was attached to while remaining on the battlefield. So if Ari had already equipped Soldevi Digger to a creature via Bludgeon Brawl's granted equip {2} ability, Soldevi Digger unattaches when Titania's Song resolves. This also matches [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #3]: an Equipment that's also a creature can't be equipped to anything.

On layers: both effects are continuous effects applied in the layer system starting from the card's printed values ([613.1a]), and each effect applies its parts in every layer it's relevant to ([613.6]) — Titania's Song in the type-changing layer, the ability-removing layer, and the power/toughness-setting layer; Bludgeon Brawl in the type-changing (subtype) and ability-adding layers. Ordering within a layer is by timestamp, but dependency can change that order ([613.2c]); here the outcome is settled by [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #2] regardless, since Bludgeon Brawl's effect checks whether the artifact is a creature.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Bludgeon Brawl was already on the battlefield when Titania's Song resolved, as stated. If instead Titania's Song were already resolved and Bludgeon Brawl entered afterward, the result is the same — Soldevi Digger is a creature, so Bludgeon Brawl never applies to it.

Two other practical notes: Soldevi Digger can attack or use {T} abilities only if Ari has continuously controlled it since the beginning of their most recent turn, no matter how recently it became a creature ([Titania's Song ruling #0]) — though with all abilities stripped it has no {T} abilities left. And if Titania's Song later leaves the battlefield, its own text says the effect continues until end of turn, so Soldevi Digger stays a 2/2 ability-less creature (and still isn't an Equipment) for the rest of that turn.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Audrey casts [Enlarge] targeting [Goblin Piker], and then attacks with the Goblin Piker. Nico blocks it with a [Baron Sengir], which has gained infect due to their [Grafted Exoskeleton] and indestructible due to their [Withstand Death]. What happens at the end of the turn?
answer:
**At end of turn, Goblin Piker dies, and Baron Sengir gets a +2/+2 counter from its own triggered ability. Baron Sengir itself survives.**

How it plays out:

**During combat.** Enlarge makes Goblin Piker 9/8 with trample (base 2/1, +7/+7) and requires it to be blocked if able; Baron Sengir blocking satisfies that. Grafted Exoskeleton makes Baron Sengir a 7/7 with infect, and Withstand Death makes it indestructible until end of turn.

- Baron Sengir deals 7 damage to Goblin Piker. Because Baron Sengir has infect, that damage isn't marked on Goblin Piker; instead Nico puts seven -1/-1 counters on Goblin Piker [702.90c]. In layer 7, Goblin Piker is 2/1 base, +7/+7 from Enlarge, -7/-7 from the counters = 2/1 [613.1g]. Its toughness is still above 0, so it survives combat [704.5f].
- Goblin Piker deals 9 damage. Audrey must assign lethal damage (7) to Baron Sengir before assigning the rest to Nico with trample, per Enlarge's granted trample; damage on Baron Sengir does nothing because Withstand Death has made it indestructible. (The detailed trample-assignment rules aren't in the provided context — I'm going off Enlarge's own reminder text.)

**The cleanup step.** All damage marked on permanents is removed and all "until end of turn" effects end *simultaneously* [514.2]. So Enlarge's +7/+7 and trample and Withstand Death's indestructible both end at the same moment the marked damage on Baron Sengir disappears — Baron Sengir is a clean, undamaged 7/7 and is in no danger.

Goblin Piker is not so lucky: the seven -1/-1 counters are permanent counters, not marked damage, so they are **not** removed at end of turn [Grafted Exoskeleton ruling #6]. Without Enlarge's boost, Goblin Piker is 2/1 minus 7/7 = -5/-6 [613.1g]. State-based actions are checked and Goblin Piker is put into Audrey's graveyard for having toughness 0 or less [704.5f].

**Baron Sengir's trigger.** Goblin Piker was dealt damage by Baron Sengir this turn and has now died, so Baron Sengir's ability triggers and puts a +2/+2 counter on it, making it a 9/9 (5/5 base, +2/+2 from Grafted Exoskeleton, +2/+2 counter). Note: the provided rules don't include the specific rule governing triggered abilities that trigger during the cleanup step, so I can't cite the exact mechanics of the extra cleanup step here, but the trigger condition is clearly met.

**Assumption on timing:** I'm assuming Withstand Death resolved before combat damage. If it were cast after combat damage was already dealt, Baron Sengir would have had 9 damage marked on a 7/7 and would have been destroyed by state-based actions before Withstand Death could save it — nothing else about the end-of-turn outcome for Goblin Piker would change, but the +2/+2 counter would have nowhere to go.

**Player count:** nothing here depends on the number of players; with more than two, only Nico (the defending player Goblin Piker attacked) would take the 2 trample damage. The provided context contains no multiplayer-specific rules that alter this.

question: Niko has a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] in their graveyard with 2 +1/+1 counters on it. Ashley controls [Containment Priest], and casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Niko. What happens?
answer:
Every creature card exiled by Ghastly Conscription — including Niko's Skullbriar, the Walking Grave — gets exiled by Containment Priest instead of arriving on the battlefield as a manifested 2/2. Ashley's Ghastly Conscription ends up doing nothing except emptying Niko's graveyard of creature cards into exile.

Step by step:

1. Ghastly Conscription resolves and exiles all creature cards from Niko's graveyard face down in a pile, shuffles the pile, and then tries to manifest them. Containment Priest doesn't stop this first exile or the shuffle — it only replaces the battlefield entry.

2. Manifesting means putting a card onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature (Ghastly Conscription ruling #8: a face-down permanent is a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, mana cost, creature types, or abilities). That means each card would enter the battlefield as a nontoken creature, and manifesting is not casting — Containment Priest's replacement effect ("If a nontoken creature would enter and it wasn't cast, exile it instead") applies to each of them. Containment Priest ruling #1 confirms the ability only spares creatures that were actually cast, and ruling #3 confirms it keys off whether the object is entering as a creature. So each card is exiled instead of entering the battlefield; none of them ever hits the battlefield, so nothing turns face up, no enters-the-battlefield abilities happen, and Ashley never gets any 2/2s.

3. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave specifically: its text "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library" is card text that overrides the normal rule that counters cease to exist on zone change, and Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1 says that ability only works if Skullbriar, the Walking Grave has the ability in the zone it's moving from. In Niko's graveyard it does have its abilities (absent something like Yixlid Jailer), so its 2 +1/+1 counters travel with it into exile with Ghastly Conscription's pile. Per Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2, those counters still adjust power/toughness outside the battlefield, so the exiled Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card is 3/3, and ruling #5 notes it retains all counter types, not just +1/+1.

4. Note that Ghastly Conscription ruling #11's "reveal a face-down permanent that leaves the battlefield" doesn't come up, since these cards never became permanents. The provided rules and rulings don't state whether the cards Containment Priest exiles end up face up or face down, so I can't settle that detail from this context.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Containment Priest is already on the battlefield when Ghastly Conscription resolves. If instead Containment Priest is flashed in after Ghastly Conscription has already finished resolving and the manifests are on the battlefield, those face-down 2/2s stay put — Containment Priest only replaces creatures entering while it's there (Containment Priest ruling #2 shows it doesn't reach back at things arriving with or before it). Conversely, if Containment Priest is flashed in while Ghastly Conscription is on the stack, it's on the battlefield at resolution and the outcome above applies.

Player count doesn't change any of this: Ghastly Conscription targets one player (Niko), and Containment Priest's replacement effect applies to any nontoken creature entering under any player's control, so the result is the same at a two-player table or a multiplayer table.

However it didn't change zones, so the counters will remain on it in exile.

question: Ashley controls [Skill Borrower] and [Sensei's Divining Top]. The top card of their library is a [Putrid Leech]. Ashley activates Skill Borrower's ability, then activates Sensei's Divining Top's first ability, choosing to put Putrid Leech second from the top. Then they activate Sensei's Divining Top again, putting Putrid Leech back on top. Can Ashley activate Skill Borrower's ability again?
answer:
Yes. Ashley can activate the gained "Pay 2 life: This creature gets +2/+2 until end of turn" ability a second time this turn, paying 2 more life (4 life total for the two activations).

Why:

1. Skill Borrower says "Play with the top card of your library revealed" and "As long as the top card of your library is an artifact or creature card, this creature has all activated abilities of that card." With Putrid Leech on top, Skill Borrower has Putrid Leech's ability, including its restriction "Activate only once each turn."

2. Rule 602.5c says that when an object acquires an activated ability that has a restriction on its use from another object, that restriction applies only to that ability as acquired from that object — it does not apply to other, identically worded abilities.

3. Rule 401.6 says that if a card is being played with revealed off the top of a library and it stops being revealed for any length of time before being revealed again, it becomes a new object. When Ashley used Sensei's Divining Top's first ability ({1}: Look at the top three cards of your library, then put them back in any order) to bury Putrid Leech second from the top, Putrid Leech stopped being revealed. When the second activation of Sensei's Divining Top's first ability put Putrid Leech back on top, it came back as a brand-new object.

4. Because it's a new object, the ability Skill Borrower now has is a new, merely identically worded ability granted by a different object. Under rule 602.5c, the "only once each turn" restriction that was already used up on the first grant doesn't carry over to it, so Skill Borrower is not prohibited from activating it (rule 602.5).

Timing assumptions: I'm assuming all of this happens in one turn (otherwise the once-per-turn restriction would reset anyway on the new turn), and that the first Skill Borrower activation fully resolved or at least was completed before Putrid Leech left the top. Note that even if the top card had changed mid-activation, the already-activated ability would still resolve normally (Skill Borrower ruling #4), and rule 401.5 means a new top card isn't revealed or lookable until the activation is finished. Also note that each Sensei's Divining Top look happens as its ability resolves; if you rearranged so Putrid Leech never actually left the revealed top card slot, no new object would be created and the restriction would still bind.

Player count doesn't matter here — nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents, so it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Noah controls a [Mons's Goblin Raiders] enchanted with a [Spider Umbra]. Alexandra casts [Yamabushi's Flame], targeting Mons's Goblin Raiders. What happens?
answer:
Mons's Goblin Raiders survives. Yamabushi's Flame deals 3 damage to it, which is lethal for a 2/2, but Spider Umbra's umbra armor replaces the destruction: all damage is removed from Mons's Goblin Raiders and Spider Umbra is destroyed instead. Because Mons's Goblin Raiders is never destroyed and never dies, Yamabushi's Flame's "exile it instead" replacement never gets to apply — nothing is exiled.

Step by step:

- Spider Umbra gives Mons's Goblin Raiders +1/+1 and reach, so it's a 2/2 while enchanted (Mons's Goblin Raiders, Spider Umbra card text).
- Yamabushi's Flame resolves and marks 3 damage on Mons's Goblin Raiders. Damage is processed into its results as modified by replacement effects [120.4c].
- Lethal damage would cause Mons's Goblin Raiders to be destroyed. Umbra armor is a static ability meaning "If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage marked on it and destroy this Aura" [702.89a]. Its effect is mandatory [Spider Umbra ruling #6], and it applies no matter why the creature would be destroyed, including lethal damage [Spider Umbra ruling #4]. Here it's the game rules about lethal damage, not Yamabushi's Flame itself, that cause Spider Umbra to be destroyed [Spider Umbra ruling #0].
- Result: Spider Umbra goes to Noah's graveyard, the 3 damage is removed from Mons's Goblin Raiders, and Mons's Goblin Raiders remains on the battlefield as a 1/1 with no damage marked (it loses the +1/+1 and reach when Spider Umbra leaves). It is not tapped and not removed from combat, since umbra armor isn't regeneration [Spider Umbra ruling #3].

One honesty note: the provided context doesn't include the rule that governs choosing between two replacement effects that would apply to the same event (umbra armor's "would be destroyed" versus Yamabushi's Flame's "would die"). The answer above follows umbra armor applying to the destruction, which is what the Spider Umbra rulings describe. If you need the tiebreak rule spelled out, that rule text isn't in the context here.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Spider Umbra was already attached when Yamabushi's Flame resolved. If Spider Umbra somehow left the battlefield before the damage was processed, there'd be no umbra armor, Mons's Goblin Raiders would die from the 3 damage, and Yamabushi's Flame would exile it instead of letting it hit the graveyard.

Player count doesn't matter: nothing here depends on the number of players, so the outcome is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: At the beginning of the game, Alex announced [Kaheera, the Orphanguard] as their companion. During the game, Alex cast [Carrion Grub] from their sideboard with [Wish]. Later, Alex restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?
answer:
**Short version: the old game just ends (no one wins or loses), and in the new game Carrion Grub is shuffled into Alex's deck — which means Alex's starting deck no longer meets Kaheera, the Orphanguard's companion condition, so Alex can't name Kaheera, the Orphanguard as their companion in the restarted game.**

**Step by step**

1. **The restart.** Karn Liberated's −14 immediately ends the current game; no player wins, loses, or draws it, and all players still in it begin a new game using the normal starting-the-game procedure [727.1] [Karn Liberated ruling #12] [Karn Liberated ruling #9]. Nothing that happened in the old game carries over [Karn Liberated ruling #1].

2. **Carrion Grub stops being a sideboard card.** Every Magic card that was involved in the game when it ended is involved in the new game, *even if it wasn't originally part of it* — the rule's own example is a card brought in from outside the game with a Wish effect, which ends up in that player's library in the new game [727.2]. Alex brought Carrion Grub in from outside the game with Wish [Wish ruling #0], so wherever Carrion Grub was when Karn Liberated resolved (battlefield, graveyard, hand, etc.), it is now part of Alex's deck and gets shuffled in as the new game begins [727.2] [Karn Liberated ruling #9]. Alex cannot swap it back out: players can't move cards between deck and sideboard before the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #5].

3. **Why that kills the companion.** A companion ability looks at your *starting deck* — your deck after sideboard cards are set aside [702.139b] — and Kaheera, the Orphanguard requires every creature card in that starting deck to be a Cat, Elemental, Nightmare, Dinosaur, or Beast. Carrion Grub is a Creature — Insect, so Alex's starting deck for the new game fails the check. The companion declaration is part of the pregame procedure and must be made fresh for the new game: before shuffling, you may reveal one card from outside the game as your companion only if your starting deck meets the requirement [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #0] [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #2]. So Kaheera, the Orphanguard is simply a sideboard card Alex owns in the new game, with no companion effect.

4. **Where Kaheera, the Orphanguard physically is.** I'm assuming Alex never paid the {3} special action to put Kaheera, the Orphanguard into hand, so it was still outside the game (the sideboard) and was never "involved in the game" — it stays outside the game [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #8]. *If instead Alex had already paid {3} and put Kaheera, the Orphanguard into hand*, it was in the game [702.139c], so under [727.2] Kaheera, the Orphanguard itself would also be shuffled into Alex's new-game library — and a card with companion sitting in your starting deck does nothing [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #7].

5. **The one way Kaheera, the Orphanguard survives as companion.** If Carrion Grub had been exiled by Karn Liberated's +4 or −3 before the −14, it is exempted from the restart procedure and is *not* in Alex's deck for the new game [727.5] [Karn Liberated ruling #6]; it stays in exile and is put onto the battlefield under Alex's control when Karn Liberated's ability finishes resolving, just before the first untap step [727.4] [Karn Liberated ruling #4] [Karn Liberated ruling #2]. In that case Alex's starting deck is still all Cats/Elementals/Nightmares/Dinosaurs/Beasts and Kaheera, the Orphanguard can be revealed as companion again — though Carrion Grub on the battlefield still won't get +1/+1 from Kaheera, the Orphanguard, since an Insect isn't one of the five listed types.

**Two players vs. multiplayer.** The above is the same either way. In multiplayer, all players still in the game when it restarts join the new game (including under the limited range of influence option) [727.7] [104.6], but anyone who had already left before the restart is not in the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #11]. Alex, as controller of the ability that restarted the game, is the starting player [Karn Liberated ruling #9], and companions are revealed starting with the starting player and proceeding in turn order [Kaheera, the Orphanguard ruling #3] — which at a multiplayer table means Alex declares (or declines) first, before the other opponents.
